Louis de Broglie was a French physicist and aristocrat who proposed a radical theory that fundamentally changed how we understand matter. He proposed that all matter possesses wave-like properties, not just light. His wave-particle duality hypothesis for matter became the foundation of wave mechanics and was experimentally confirmed through the diffraction of electrons. He won the 1929 Nobel Prize in Physics for his discovery of the wave nature of electrons.

In his 1924 doctoral thesis, de Broglie formulated what became known as the de Broglie hypothesis. He proposed that a moving particle has an associated wavelength determined by a simple equation: the wavelength equals Planck's constant divided by the particle's momentum. This insight suddenly unified the wave and particle pictures of nature — everything that moves has a wavelength.

De Broglie's hypothesis explained the quantized orbits in Niels Bohr's atomic model by demonstrating that the stable electron orbits around a nucleus correspond to standing waves. If an electron wave must form a complete loop around the nucleus, only certain wavelengths fit perfectly, which naturally explains why electrons occupy only specific discrete energy levels. This was a stunning bridge between Bohr's earlier model and quantum theory.

He developed the pilot wave theory, also called the double solution theory, which was an early deterministic and non-local hidden-variable interpretation of quantum mechanics. This approach was later expanded by David Bohm into what is now called Bohmian mechanics. De Broglie's predictions were experimentally confirmed by the Davisson-Germer experiment, in which electrons were scattered by a nickel crystal and showed the same diffraction patterns as light, demonstrating conclusively that electrons truly do behave as waves.

In 1952, de Broglie was awarded the Kalinga Prize by UNESCO for his efforts in popularizing scientific knowledge. Albert Einstein endorsed de Broglie's doctoral thesis, which was crucial for gaining acceptance among other physicists. Erwin Schrödinger used de Broglie's concept of matter waves as the inspiration for constructing his famous wave equation of quantum mechanics.
